videoIdeas.title: The room beats the medal
videoIdeas.hook: You keep waiting to be the best in the room. That's why you're still outside it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your highest-performing post ever ('Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' — 909 views) proves this exact angle lands for your audience. Lean back into the 'showing up beats being the best' theme while it's clearly working, and expand it from running into a wider mindset lesson.
videoIdeas.script:
You keep waiting to be the best in the room. That's why you're still outside it.

I run half marathons. I am nowhere near the fastest. People overtake me the whole way. And for a while that used to kill me.

Then I realised something. Everyone who overtook me and everyone behind me — we all have one thing in common. We entered. The guy sitting on his sofa judging all of us? He didn't.

Being in the room is the entry fee. You don't get to compete, lead, or win anything from the outside. Stop auditing whether you're good enough to show up. Show up first. Get good in the room.

You were never going to be ready before you entered. Nobody is.

visuals.setting: Film outdoors in running gear, slightly out of breath, natural daylight, handheld or propped phone. Real, not polished. Medium shot so viewers see the effort on your face.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, breathing hard, then you stop and turn to camera with on-screen text: 'Dead last. Still here.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: freeze-frame of runners overtaking you with text 'count how many pass me'
Show a finisher's medal in hand then toss it aside: 'this isn't the point'
On-screen text punchline that contradicts the visual: standing still while text reads 'moving forward'

videoIdeas.title: Speak like you've already lost the fear
videoIdeas.hook: Most people don't have a public speaking problem. They have a 'what will they think of me' problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is a core pillar in your brief but absent from your top posts. Competitors win with sharp, reframe-style value content (saffanabanana's whiteboard, doctordaanish's lists). A blunt reframe on speaking fear fills your own content gap and plays to a pillar you own.
videoIdeas.script:
Most people don't have a public speaking problem. They have a 'what will they think of me' problem.

Your voice doesn't shake because the words are hard. It shakes because you've handed a room full of strangers the power to decide your worth.

Here's the fix, and it's not a breathing exercise. Before you speak, decide what you're actually there to do. Not to impress them. To give them something. The second your job becomes 'deliver this point clearly' instead of 'don't look stupid,' the fear has nothing to hold onto.

Nervousness is just self-focus wearing a costume. Point it at the message, not at yourself.

You'll still feel it. You'll just stop obeying it.

visuals.setting: Indoors, clean background, shirt or smart-casual, standing and speaking directly to camera with calm authority — embody the point. Steady framing, chest-up shot.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a tight shot of your hands, deliberately still, with on-screen text: 'this used to shake.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start mid-sentence as if already presenting, then cut to you addressing camera
On-screen text punchline: 'it's not fear of speaking' / beat / 'it's fear of them'
Cold open with a shaky voice clip then cut sharply to steady delivery

videoIdeas.title: Leaders who need to be liked
videoIdeas.hook: If you need everyone to like you, you will never lead anyone.
videoIdeas.rationale: Leadership is a named pillar but missing from your posts. Your activism post on Majid Freeman (289 likes) shows your audience responds to conviction and taking a stance. A blunt leadership take on the cost of being liked matches that proven appetite for principle-driven content.
videoIdeas.script:
If you need everyone to like you, you will never lead anyone.

Leadership and popularity are not the same job. One is about making people comfortable. The other is about taking people somewhere — and people rarely want to move.

The moment you make a real decision, someone is going to be unhappy. If your instinct in that moment is to soften it, water it down, make it palatable to the loudest complainer — you're not leading. You're negotiating with your own fear of rejection.

The Prophet ﷺ was called a liar and a madman by his own people. He didn't lead by consensus. He led by truth, and the respect came after.

You don't need to be liked. You need to be trusted. Those are built very differently.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing indoors, calm and grounded, darker/neutral tones to match the serious tone. Minimal movement, strong eye contact. Let the words carry it.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a close, unsmiling shot with on-screen text: 'stop trying to be liked.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: nod and smile at camera, then cut to flat expression as you deliver the hook
On-screen text that builds: 'liked' crossed out, replaced with 'trusted'
Cold open mid-point: 'someone is going to be unhappy with your decision — good.'

videoIdeas.title: 5 habits I'd drop if I were 18 again
videoIdeas.hook: 5 things I did at 18 that quietly wasted years. Number 3 still gets me.
videoIdeas.rationale: The listicle format is dominating your niche right now — doctordaanish's '5 careers I don't want' hit 161k views and '5 specialties' 30k. You have zero list-format content. Borrow the structure that's clearly working and load it with your blunt, specific voice.
videoIdeas.script:
5 things I did at 18 that quietly wasted years.

One. Waiting to feel motivated. Motivation is a mood, not a strategy. The work happens whether you feel like it or not.

Two. Keeping my goals private so no one could watch me fail. All that did was make it easy to quit silently.

Three. Confusing being busy with being useful. I filled my days and moved nothing forward. This one still gets me.

Four. Picking friends by comfort instead of direction. The people around you set your ceiling. I set mine low for years.

Five. Treating my deen as the thing I'd get serious about 'later.' Later is not promised, and everything else is built on that foundation anyway.

If you're 18 now — you have the one thing I can't buy back. Time. Don't spend it the way I did.

visuals.setting: Clean, well-lit talking-head setup, smart-casual. Use quick cuts on each number to keep pace. On-screen number counter for each point. Energetic but controlled.
visuals.visualHook: Open with bold on-screen text '#3 still gets me' over a tight face shot, holding up a hand counting.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start at number 3 out of order, then 'let me back up'
On-screen numbered captions that snap in with each point for retention
Cold open: 'I wasted years on number two' before listing anything

videoIdeas.title: Silence is a decision
videoIdeas.hook: When you say nothing to stay safe, you've already picked a side. The wrong one.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Majid Freeman post (289 likes, your highest like count) shows your audience deeply values moral courage framed through faith. Lifeofdinoo and saffanabanana both win big with principled stance content. This extends your proven theme into a leadership lesson on moral courage.
videoIdeas.script:
When you say nothing to stay safe, you've already picked a side. The wrong one.

The Prophet ﷺ said: whoever sees an injustice, let him change it with his hand, or his tongue, or his heart. Notice there's no fourth option. There's no 'or stay quiet and protect your image.'

We've convinced ourselves that neutrality is maturity. It isn't. Neutrality in the face of oppression is just comfort wearing a suit. The oppressor never needs you to agree with him. He just needs you to stay quiet.

Speaking up costs something. Followers, invitations, approval. That's the point. If it was free, it wouldn't be courage.

You don't have to be loud. You have to be honest. Start there.

visuals.setting: Serious tone, indoors, neutral clothing, steady close-up. Low-key lighting. Let the delivery be measured, not shouty — conviction, not anger.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a silent, held stare at camera for a beat, then on-screen text: 'saying nothing is saying something.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: mouth taped or hand over mouth visual, then removed as you start
On-screen text punchline: 'neutral' redefined as 'on the oppressor's side'
Cold open with the hadith text on a black screen before you appear

videoIdeas.title: The real reason you procrastinate
videoIdeas.hook: You're not lazy. You're scared the thing won't be good enough — so you never finish it.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's journaling self-improvement post pulled 24k views and lifeofdinoo's 'you can pray and still need help' shows honest psychological takes resonate. You have strong relatable moments (the running posts, the burnout/Sabr app topic). A blunt reframe on procrastination fits your burnout territory and your voice.
videoIdeas.script:
You're not lazy. You're scared the thing won't be good enough — so you never start it.

Procrastination gets sold as a discipline problem. It's rarely that. It's usually fear in disguise. As long as the project stays in your head, it's perfect. The moment you start, it becomes real, flawed, and judgeable. So you avoid it to protect the fantasy.

The fix isn't a better morning routine. It's lowering the stakes. Tell yourself you're going to do a bad first version. Deliberately bad. Ugly draft, messy first attempt, embarrassing rep one.

You can't edit a blank page. You can't improve a workout you never did. Done badly beats perfect in your head, every single time.

Start ugly. Fix it later.

visuals.setting: Relatable, slightly casual setting — desk or home, natural light. Conversational older-brother energy, leaning in. Medium shot, a bit more relaxed than the leadership videos.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a blank page or empty screen with on-screen text: 'this is what fear looks like.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: scribble something messy on paper then hold it up — 'start this ugly'
On-screen text punchline: 'you're not lazy' / beat / 'you're scared'
Cold open mid-action crossing out a to-do list item you never did

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post for a reason — 909 views, 115 likes, 11 comments, by far your strongest engagement. The line 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its best: short, punchy, a reframe that doubles as a life lesson while being literally true about running. It's relatable and quotable, which is why it pulled comments.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the insight implicit. Add one line in the caption that pulls the metaphor out explicitly ('showing up is the entry fee most people never pay') so the mindset lesson reaches people who don't run. Also pin this as a series — you've found a vein (running as a lens for mindset), so mine it repeatedly instead of treating it as a one-off.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 437 views and your second-best reach. Islamic history as a hook works — the specific date '711 AD' and the counterintuitive detail (Christians welcoming Muslims) is a strong, concrete opener that stops the scroll. This fits your niche and shows your audience has appetite for history-with-a-point.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite decent views means it informed but didn't provoke. History alone is a lecture; tie it to a present-day lesson for the viewer ('leadership that liberates vs leadership that extracts — which are you building?') and end on a question so people reply. The caption also got cut off mid-sentence — front-load the payoff before the fold.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 376 views, 45 likes, 5 comments — strong engagement ratio for the reach. 'Never running through a park at night ever again 😭' is short, human, and funny. It shows personality and relatability, which your audience clearly rewards. These unpolished personal moments punch above their weight.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This is pure relatability with no takeaway — fine occasionally, but it doesn't build your authority in any pillar. Use these personal moments as a Trojan horse: open with the funny park story, then pivot to a mindset point (e.g. on fear, risk, or awareness). You get the hook of relatability and the retention payoff of value.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 209 views on a genuinely useful topic. Opening with 'Burnout affects so many of us, whether you're a medical student or not' is a smart inclusive hook that widens the audience beyond one niche. Burnout is a proven winner — doctordaanish's journaling/mental-health content does huge numbers.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This reads like an app promo, and the drop in engagement shows it. The Sabr mention makes it feel like an ad, which kills reach. Lead with your own blunt take on burnout and what actually helped you first; earn the attention, then mention the tool at the very end as a P.S. Value first, product last — never the reverse.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count of any post. This proves your audience responds powerfully to moral conviction grounded in faith. Opening with the clear call ('We must speak out') plus the hadith gives it authority and emotional weight. This is a core part of your identity and it clearly resonates.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (carousel), not video — and video is dominating your niche across every competitor. Repackage this exact message as a talking-head reel where you deliver the hadith and the stance to camera; the conviction lands far harder with your voice and face. Also only 1 comment despite high likes — end with a direct ask ('what's stopping you from speaking up?') to convert passive agreement into conversation.
